# Ānāpāna Saṁyutta (SN 54)

**ID:** SN 54  
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Ānāpāna Saṁyutta  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0305m.mul9.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0305m.mul9.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ānāpāna Saṁyutta* (SN 54), translated as the "Linked Discourses on Breath Meditation," is the fifty-fourth section of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, situated within the *Mahāvagga* [Gethin 2001; Bodhi 2005]. The collection centers on mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*), revered as the primary meditation practiced by the Buddha himself before and after his awakening, and characterized as a peaceful dwelling (*tathāgatavihāra*) that stills discursive thoughts and trembling of the body [Gethin 2001; Bodhi 2005; Wen 2011]. Whereas other discourses treat breath awareness in a simple four-step formula, the suttas of SN 54 systematically expand it into sixteen steps or facets arranged into four tetrads [Bodhi 2005]. These four tetrads correspond directly to the four establishments of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), which in turn sequentially arouse and fulfill the seven factors of awakening (*bojjhaṅga*) [Gethin 2001; Bodhi 2005; Wen 2011].

Individual discourses highlight various doctrinal themes and historical episodes. In the *Ekadhamma Sutta* (SN 54.1), the basic practice formula is laid out [Polak 2011]. The *Mahākappina Sutta* (SN 54.7) describes how developing the "concentration of mindfulness of breathing" (*ānāpānasati-samādhi*) results in complete bodily and mental stillness [Wen 2011; Anālayo 2019]. In the *Vesālī Sutta* (SN 54.9), mindfulness of breathing is introduced by the Buddha as a peaceful remedy after a group of monastics engaged in foulness meditation (*asubha*) developed excessive revulsion toward their bodies and committed suicide [Anālayo 2018; Radich 2007; Wen 2011]. Other discourses, such as the *Kaṅkheyya Sutta* (SN 54.12) and the *Paṭhamaānanda Sutta* (SN 54.13), explicate training in relation to abandoning the hindrances and sequentially cultivating the awakening factors [Anālayo 2019; Wen 2011].

**Sources**

- [Gethin 2001] R. M. Gethin, The Buddhist Path to Awakening (2001) — Place of the saṁyutta in the Mahāvagga and relationship between ānāpānasati, satipaṭṭhāna, and bojjhaṅgas.
- [Bodhi 2005] Bhikkhu Bodhi, In the Buddha's Words (2005) — Identification of breath meditation as the Buddha's dwelling and the sixteen-step formula aligned with four tetrads.
- [Anālayo 2017] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Meditator's Life of the Buddha (2017) — Parallels to SN 54.11 in SĀ 803 and Chinese Āgamas.
- [Anālayo 2018] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Satipatthana Meditation: A Practice Guide (2018) — Discussion of SN 54.9 (monks' suicides at Vesālī) and awakening factor arousal in SN 54.16.
- [Anālayo 2019] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Mindfulness of Breathing: A Practice Guide and Translations (2019) — Analysis of ānāpānasati-samādhi in SN 54.7, Vinaya versions of SN 54.9, training regarding hindrances in SN 54.12, and Ānanda suttas (SN 54.13–14).
- [Polak 2011] Grzegorz Polak, Reexamining Jhana (2011) — Significance of SN 54 in the Suttapiṭaka and basic formula in Ekadhamma Sutta (SN 54.1).
- [Radich 2007] Michael David Radich, The Somatics of Liberation (2007) — Narrative summary of SN 54.9 at Vesālī and chronological observations on Mahāvagga samyuttas.
- [Wen] Tzungkuen Wen, A Study of Sukkhavipassaka in Pali Buddhism — Discussion of SN 54.7, SN 54.9, and the fulfillment of the enlightenment factors in SN 54.13.
